source:
Build a Complete Roblox MVP: 3D Friendly-Fire Tower Defense Game

Act as a senior Roblox gameplay engineer, technical designer, UI engineer, and optimization specialist. Build a complete, playable Roblox Studio MVP for an original 3D game inspired by the mechanical concept of towers whose projectiles can also harm the player.

Do not copy copyrighted names, characters, artwork, maps, dialogue, music, UI, or other identifiable assets from any existing game. Create an original project using the temporary working title:

Friendly Fire Foundry

The goal is to produce a polished, playable vertical slice rather than merely explaining how it could be built.

Core concept

The player controls an engineer who is physically present in a 3D tower-defense arena.

Enemies follow a fixed route toward a core. The player places automated defensive towers that fire projectiles at enemies. Those same tower projectiles can hit and damage the player.

Destroyed enemies drop physical scrap pickups. The player must move into dangerous areas to collect that scrap and use it to construct more towers.

The resulting loop is:

1. Build defensive towers.
2. Towers destroy enemies.
3. Towers also fill the arena with dangerous projectiles.
4. Enemies drop scrap.
5. The player enters dangerous areas to collect scrap.
6. The player spends scrap on more towers.
7. More towers create more firepower and more danger.
8. Survive all waves without losing the player or the core.

The central design principle is:

«Increasing defensive power must also make the arena more dangerous for the player.»

Required final result

Produce a Roblox Studio experience in which one player can:

- Spawn into a complete arena.
- Move using keyboard, gamepad, or mobile controls.
- Use a fixed isometric 3D camera.
- Place three different tower types.
- Fight three different enemy types.
- Survive ten waves.
- Dodge projectiles fired by their own towers.
- Collect physical scrap drops.
- Use a wrench to damage and knock enemies backward.
- Sell towers.
- Win by completing wave ten.
- Lose by dying or allowing the core to be destroyed.
- Restart the match from a results screen.

Do not stop at a design document. Implement the actual systems, scripts, instances, user interface, placeholder models, effects, and complete match loop.

Development rules

Use the following engineering standards:

- Use Luau with "--!strict" wherever practical.
- Use modular service/controller architecture.
- Keep the server authoritative over all gameplay.
- Treat every client request as untrusted.
- Use data-driven tower, enemy, and wave definitions.
- Use centralized update loops rather than one loop per entity.
- Avoid relying on "Touched" for fast-moving projectiles.
- Do not create a server-controlled physical Part for every projectile.
- Separate server projectile simulation from client projectile rendering.
- Use object pooling for frequently created visual objects.
- Use attributes for replicated state when appropriate.
- Use "CollectionService" tags for build zones, hitboxes, and blockers.
- Use collision groups to simplify projectile queries.
- Avoid external frameworks unless they are already available and clearly necessary.
- Do not require paid assets or plugins.
- Use original placeholder geometry if final assets are unavailable.
- Prioritize a fully working gameplay loop over visual complexity.
- Do not leave major systems as pseudocode or TODO comments.
- Make sensible decisions without repeatedly requesting clarification.
- Comment complex code and explain important architectural choices.

MVP scope

Include:

- One player per server.
- One complete arena.
- Ten authored waves.
- Three tower types.
- Three enemy types.
- One currency called Scrap.
- One wrench attack.
- Physical scrap pickups.
- Player health.
- Core health.
- Tower placement and selling.
- Build and combat phases.
- Victory and defeat screens.
- Keyboard and mouse support.
- Gamepad support.
- Mobile support.
- Basic effects, sounds, animations, and readable UI.

Do not include:

- Multiplayer co-op.
- Matchmaking.
- DataStore persistence.
- Permanent progression.
- Tower upgrade trees.
- Daily rewards.
- Pets.
- Trading.
- Multiple maps.
- Multiple currencies.
- Battle passes.
- Loot boxes.
- Complex inventory systems.
- Endless mode.
- Story mode.
- Procedural maps.
- Monetization systems.

Structure the code so that multiplayer and additional content could be added later, but do not implement them for the MVP.

Gameplay specification

Player

The player is an engineer physically present in the arena.

Starting values:

- Maximum combat health: 5.
- Starting combat health: 5.
- Walk speed: approximately 18 studs per second.
- Jumping disabled.
- Starting Scrap: 100.
- Post-hit invulnerability: 0.75 seconds.
- Maximum placed towers: 12.
- Tower placement range: 22 studs from the player.

Do not rely directly on ordinary Humanoid health for the match combat system. Store and manage custom combat health on the server using player attributes or a dedicated state record.

Recommended player attributes:

- "Scrap"
- "CombatHealth"
- "MaxCombatHealth"
- "InvulnerableUntil"
- "TowersPlaced"

The player loses immediately when combat health reaches zero.

Core

The core is located at the end of the enemy path.

Starting values:

- Maximum health: 10.
- Starting health: 10.

Enemies damage the core when their path progress reaches the endpoint. Do not rely on physical collisions with the core.

The player loses immediately when core health reaches zero.

Match phases

Implement a finite-state match controller with these phases:

- "Waiting"
- "Build"
- "Combat"
- "Victory"
- "Defeat"

Use one centralized service to control phase transitions.

The match sequence is:

1. Initialize or reset the map.
2. Spawn the player.
3. Enter the first Build phase.
4. Allow the player to place towers.
5. Start the wave when the player presses Start Wave.
6. Enter Combat.
7. Spawn all scheduled enemies.
8. Wait until all scheduled enemies have spawned and all living enemies are gone.
9. Enter the next Build phase.
10. Repeat until wave ten is cleared.
11. Enter Victory.
12. Enter Defeat immediately if the player or core reaches zero health.
13. Show a results screen with a Restart button.

After the first wave, Build phases may include a ten-second auto-start timer. The player must be allowed to begin the next wave early.

Players may continue placing and selling towers during Combat.

Recommended replicated match attributes

Create a replicated match-state Folder or Configuration under Workspace.

Use attributes such as:

- "Phase"
- "Wave"
- "MaxWaves"
- "CoreHealth"
- "CoreMaxHealth"
- "EnemiesAlive"
- "EnemiesRemainingToSpawn"
- "BuildTimeRemaining"
- "Result"

The UI should listen to attribute changes.

Camera and controls

Camera

Use a fixed, scriptable, isometric-style 3D camera.

Recommended starting settings:

- "CameraType = Scriptable"
- Field of view: 60 degrees.
- Offset from player: approximately "Vector3.new(34, 52, 42)".
- Downward viewing angle: approximately 55-65 degrees.
- Smooth follow.
- Fixed world rotation.
- No player-controlled camera rotation in the MVP.
- Slight look-ahead toward the aim point, clamped to avoid pushing the player near the edge of the screen.

The camera must prioritize visibility of:

- Incoming projectiles.
- The player.
- Nearby towers.
- The enemy path.
- Scrap pickups.
- Placement locations.

The map should remain mostly planar. Do not make jumping or vertical projectile dodging part of the MVP.

Keyboard and mouse controls

Use approximately:

- WASD: move.
- Mouse position: aim and placement cursor.
- Left click: place tower or swing wrench.
- Right click or Escape: cancel placement.
- 1: select Sentry.
- 2: select Scatter Tower.
- 3: select Pulse Tower.
- Q: select wrench.
- Space: start wave during Build.
- X or Delete: sell selected tower.

Prevent one input from accidentally triggering multiple actions. For example, confirming tower placement must not simultaneously swing the wrench.

Gamepad controls

Use approximately:

- Left stick: movement.
- Right stick: aim cursor.
- Right trigger: confirm placement or swing wrench.
- B: cancel placement.
- D-pad: select tower.
- Y: start wave.
- X: sell tower.

Create a world-space or screen-space aiming cursor for gamepad users.

Mobile controls

Provide:

- Roblox movement thumbstick.
- Large wrench button.
- Tower hotbar.
- Start Wave button.
- Tap terrain to position or confirm tower placement.
- Cancel placement button.
- Tap an existing tower to select it.
- Sell button for selected towers.

Do not require manual camera gestures on mobile.

Use "ContextActionService" or another centralized input layer so actions can be rebound by platform.

Arena design

Build one original greybox-to-polished arena.

Recommended dimensions:

- Overall arena: approximately 120 by 120 studs.
- Enemy path width: 9-12 studs.
- Tower range: approximately 30-50 studs.
- Main action takes place on one horizontal plane.

The enemy route should include:

1. A long straightaway where towers can fire along the path.
2. A perpendicular crossing where tower fire can cut across the player's movement route.
3. A central bend or loop where radial towers become powerful but hazardous.
4. Several build areas with visibly different risk profiles.
5. Open spaces that allow projectile dodging.
6. No tall geometry that frequently hides the player or bullets.

Create the following Workspace structure:

- "Workspace.Map"
 - "Geometry"
 - "BuildZones"
 - "PlacementBlockers"
 - "EnemyPath"
 - "Spawn"
 - "Core"
- "Workspace.Runtime"
 - "Towers"
 - "Enemies"
 - "Pickups"
 - "Effects"
- "Workspace.MatchState"

The enemy path should consist of ordered waypoint Parts. Give them numeric names or an "Order" attribute.

Use invisible blocker volumes to prevent towers from being placed on:

- The enemy path.
- The core.
- Map boundaries.
- Decorative obstacles.
- Other prohibited areas.

Enemy movement

Do not use "PathfindingService" for the fixed enemy route.

Precompute a polyline path using the ordered waypoint Parts.

For every path segment, store:

- Start position.
- End position.
- Segment length.
- Cumulative starting distance.

Represent each enemy's route progress using a scalar "PathDistance".

Each enemy record should contain at least:

- Unique ID.
- Enemy type.
- Model.
- Current health.
- Maximum health.
- Speed.
- Path distance.
- Current velocity.
- Alive state.

Move anchored enemy models kinematically along the path.

Use one centralized enemy update loop running around 20-30 times per second.

For each enemy:

1. Increase "PathDistance" by "Speed * deltaTime".
2. Sample the path at the new distance.
3. Move and rotate the model.
4. Update its velocity.
5. If it reaches the total path length, damage the core and remove the enemy.

Maintain an authoritative dictionary of active enemies. Do not repeatedly scan all enemy instances from every tower.

Enemy types

Implement these three enemy archetypes.

Scrapper

- Maximum health: 30.
- Speed: 8 studs per second.
- Core damage: 1.
- Scrap drop: 10.
- Medium hit radius.
- Basic enemy.

Runner

- Maximum health: 18.
- Speed: 14 studs per second.
- Core damage: 1.
- Scrap drop: 8.
- Small hit radius.
- Fast and difficult for slow projectiles to hit.

Brute

- Maximum health: 120.
- Speed: 4.5 studs per second.
- Core damage: 3.
- Scrap drop: 25.
- Large hit radius.
- Slow tank enemy.

Every enemy should have:

- Original placeholder model.
- Readable silhouette.
- Health indicator when damaged or targeted.
- Hit feedback.
- Death effect.
- Server-created Scrap pickup on death.

Dead enemies must never:

- Damage the core.
- Drop Scrap more than once.
- Receive further damage.
- Remain targetable.

Towers

Use data-driven tower definitions. Do not place independent scripts inside every tower model.

Each tower record should contain:

- Unique ID.
- Tower type.
- Model.
- Position.
- Owner user ID.
- Next allowed fire time.
- Optional current target.

Use one centralized tower update loop.

For every tower ready to fire:

1. Find a valid target.
2. Rotate the turret head toward the target.
3. Play an attack telegraph if required.
4. Spawn logical projectiles.
5. Set the next fire time.

Use simple predictive aiming:

1. Estimate travel time using distance divided by projectile speed.
2. Clamp lead time to approximately 0.6 seconds.
3. Add enemy velocity multiplied by predicted travel time.
4. Aim toward the predicted position.

Tower 1: Sentry

Starting values:

- Cost: 50 Scrap.
- Range: 45 studs.
- Damage: 15.
- Fire interval: 0.75 seconds.
- Projectile speed: 80 studs per second.
- Projectile radius: 0.7 studs.
- Projectile lifetime: 2.5 seconds.
- Projectiles per attack: 1.
- Targeting mode: enemy with greatest path progress.
- Hazard rating: low.

Behavior:

- Fires one accurate projectile.
- Best for long lanes.
- Easy to understand.
- Introduced first.

Tower 2: Scatter Tower

Starting values:

- Cost: 80 Scrap.
- Range: 30 studs.
- Damage: 6 per projectile.
- Fire interval: 1.35 seconds.
- Projectile speed: 68 studs per second.
- Projectile radius: approximately 0.65 studs.
- Projectile lifetime: 2.1 seconds.
- Projectiles per attack: 5.
- Total spread: 18 degrees.
- Targeting mode: nearest enemy.
- Hazard rating: medium.

Behavior:

- Fires a five-projectile cone centered on the target.
- Strong at close range.
- Particularly dangerous when the player stands between the tower and path.

Tower 3: Pulse Tower

Starting values:

- Cost: 120 Scrap.
- Range: 35 studs.
- Damage: 10 per projectile.
- Fire interval: 2.6 seconds.
- Projectile speed: 58 studs per second.
- Projectile radius: 0.8 studs.
- Projectile lifetime: 2.4 seconds.
- Projectiles per attack: 8.
- Pattern: evenly spaced radial burst.
- Hazard rating: high.

Behavior:

- Fires in eight horizontal directions whenever at least one enemy is in range.
- Telegraphs the burst for approximately 0.35 seconds.
- Uses a charge glow, contracting ring, and warning sound.
- Powerful near bends and central areas.
- Creates substantial danger for the player.

Tower targeting

Implement at least:

- "First": valid enemy in range with greatest "PathDistance".
- "Nearest": valid enemy in range with the smallest squared distance.

Use squared distance checks when possible.

Do not create an independent infinite loop or Heartbeat connection for every tower.

Suggested update frequency:

- Target and fire checks: 10-20 times per second.
- Visual turret rotation may interpolate on the client for smoothness.

Projectile architecture

This system is critical.

Do not use ordinary unanchored physics Parts with "Touched" as the authoritative projectile system.

Each projectile must have:

Server-side logical representation

Store:

- Unique ID.
- Current position.
- Previous position.
- Velocity.
- Collision radius.
- Damage.
- Expiration time.
- Visual style.
- Alive state.

The server must:

- Spawn logical projectiles.
- Advance them using a centralized fixed-step update.
- Perform swept collision checks.
- Apply damage.
- Remove projectiles on impact or expiration.
- Notify clients of spawn and removal.

Recommended simulation rate:

- Approximately 30 Hz.

Client-side visual representation

The client must:

- Obtain visual projectile objects from a pool.
- Position them using origin, velocity, spawn time, and synchronized server time.
- Animate them every render frame.
- Play trails and visual effects.
- Return them to the pool when removed.

Do not send projectile position updates every frame.

On projectile spawn, replicate only necessary data such as:

- Projectile ID.
- Origin.
- Velocity.
- Radius.
- Style.
- Server spawn time.

On removal, replicate:

- Projectile ID.
- Removal reason.
- Final impact position if relevant.

Use "Workspace:GetServerTimeNow()" to keep client visuals approximately synchronized.

Projectile collision

Use swept collision from previous position to new position.

Use "Workspace:Spherecast" when available, or an equivalent reliable swept-radius query.

Projectile queries should detect:

- World geometry.
- Player hitbox.
- Enemy hitboxes.

Projectile queries should ignore:

- The firing tower.
- Decorative player body parts.
- Decorative enemy body parts.
- Pickups.
- Non-gameplay visual effects.

A projectile should affect the first valid object in its movement segment and then be removed.

The same projectile must be capable of:

- Damaging an enemy.
- Damaging the player.
- Being destroyed by world geometry.

Tower projectiles should deal their configured damage to enemies, but normally one combat-health point to the player unless deliberately balanced otherwise.

Collision proxies and groups

Create simplified invisible hitboxes.

Player hitbox

Use one invisible Part welded to or following the HumanoidRootPart.

Recommended values:

- Approximate size: "Vector3.new(3, 4, 3)".
- "Transparency = 1".
- "CanCollide = false".
- "CanTouch = false".
- "CanQuery = true".

Enemy hitbox

Use one invisible hitbox or root proxy per enemy.

Recommended properties:

- Anchored.
- Non-collidable.
- Non-touchable.
- Queryable.
- Size appropriate to enemy archetype.

Use attributes such as:

- "EntityKind"
- "EnemyId"
- "UserId"

Create collision groups such as:

- "World"
- "CharacterBody"
- "PlayerHitbox"
- "EnemyBody"
- "EnemyHitbox"
- "Tower"
- "Pickup"
- "ProjectileQuery"

Configure projectile queries so only relevant gameplay groups are considered.

Use "PhysicsService" and initialize collision groups safely at server startup.

Player damage

Use a server-side damage service.

When a projectile hits the player:

1. Verify that the match is active.
2. Check the player's invulnerability timestamp.
3. Subtract one combat-health point if not invulnerable.
4. Set "InvulnerableUntil" to current server time plus 0.75 seconds.
5. Trigger client feedback.
6. Enter Defeat if health reaches zero.

Player hit feedback should include:

- Brief character flash.
- Short hit sound.
- Small camera impulse.
- Heart UI animation.
- Brief screen-edge effect.
- Visible invulnerability flicker.

Do not use large camera shake that makes bullets difficult to read.

Scrap economy

Enemies must drop physical Scrap pickups at their death positions.

Each enemy should normally create one pickup representing the enemy's full Scrap value.

Pickup behavior:

- Spawn near enemy death position.
- Add small random horizontal offset.
- Hover and rotate visually.
- Remain for 12-15 seconds.
- Begin magnet behavior within approximately 8 studs.
- Collect within approximately 2.5 studs.
- Add Scrap on the server.
- Play a collection effect.
- Remove exactly once.

Recommended economy values:

- Starting Scrap: 100.
- Wave completion reward: "20 + 5 * waveNumber".
- Tower sale refund: 70% of base cost.
- No interest system.
- No passive income.
- No automatic currency for enemy deaths without collection.

Use a centralized pickup update loop around 10 Hz.

The pickup collection process must be server-authoritative.

Wrench combat

Give the player a wrench attack.

Starting behavior:

- Cooldown: 0.65 seconds.
- Maximum range: 7 studs.
- Horizontal cone.
- Cone half-angle of approximately 55 degrees.
- Damage: 4.
- Knockback: subtract 5 studs from the enemy's "PathDistance".
- Clamp path distance to zero or greater.

Use a server-authoritative cone test based on:

- Player root position.
- Valid aim direction.
- Distance to enemy.
- Dot product threshold.

Do not use physical impulses for enemy knockback. Modify path progress directly.

The wrench should:

- Damage enemies.
- Push enemies backward.
- Play an original swing animation.
- Play a visible arc effect.
- Play impact feedback when it hits.
- Never damage the player, towers, or core.

Do not implement projectile reflection in the MVP unless every required MVP system is already complete and stable.

answers.ask: The title suggests an industrial foundry, but no art direction was given - should the arena read as a working foundry, or stay neutral greybox?
answers.answer: Make it a compact, stylized industrial foundry arena: metal platforms, pipes, furnaces, conveyor-like route elements, and warm orange molten-metal lighting, using original low-poly placeholder geometry.
